title: Rapport de Prospective du GDR Recherche Opérationnelle et Décision (ROD)
contribution: French community roadmap for operations research (68 writers); Leyffer co-writes only §B.2.2, a questionnaire-based synthesis of solver developers' views on solver limits (scale, NLP degeneracy, formulation, openness vs performance, parallelism, uncertainty) and remedies (composability, structure detection, interpretable ML, GPU, complementarity support in NLP).
problem_entry: Written for the 2025 renewal of GDR ROD (p. 3); §B.2.2 enters via a questionnaire of 29 April 2025 to solver developers, gated on license, packaging, lasting repository, docs and CI/tests, with six questions (pp. 31-32).
key_idea: Synthesis in question order: define solver/modeller/meta-solver (p. 32); limits: scale, NLP degeneracy with redundant constraints or max(x,y), formulation expertise, openness vs performance, parallel/GPU, uncertainty (pp. 33, 35); remedies: composability, structure detection, interpretable ML, GPU SIMD, NLP sparse linear algebra and complementarity support (pp. 35-36).
assumptions: Self-selected respondents passing the eligibility gate (p. 31); 16 tools in Table 1 incl. Uno and MadNLP as NLP-only codes (p. 34); qualitative synthesis with no per-solver attribution and only two numeric thresholds (pp. 32-33).
proof_devices: n/a: no theorems or proofs in the report (pp. 1-77)
positioning: Cross-references §B.1.1, §B.1.4, §B.2.1 (p. 32); cites software URLs only (pp. 34-35); sceptical of generic deep learning in solvers, positive on narrow interpretable models (p. 35). Non-Leyffer §B.1.1 favours direct NLP solving over linearization and complementarity/vanishing constraints (pp. 12-13).
writing: French committee prose following the questionnaire order (p. 32); run-in headings (pp. 32, 33, 35); hedged attribution to respondents (pp. 33-34, 36); no conclusion (p. 36).
limits_future: No self-stated limits; visible: self-selected sample, no attribution, little quantitative data (pp. 31-36). Directions: composability, structure detection, interpretable ML, GPU, NLP linear algebra and complementarity, CP linear arithmetic, research-engineer support (pp. 35-36).

method_links.note: Collective voice: openness to external components trades against performance (structure lost); remedies call for component integration and solver composability. Matches Method 1's building blocks and its 'owning the tree can cost speed' limitation; Leyffer's share not separable.
Collective voice: non-equivalent formulations differ in solve time; NLP degeneracy from redundant constraints or nonsmooth max(x,y) causes instability.
Weak, collective voice: complementarity support in NLP solvers named as remedy for degeneracy; Uno among surveyed NLP solvers.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Questionnaire gated on license, packaging, repository, docs, CI/tests, six fixed questions, synthesis in question order; single collective occurrence.

transferable: Gate a field survey on software-quality criteria (license, packaging, lasting repository, docs, CI/tests) and synthesize in question order (pp. 31-32).
Classify a solver failure as scale, numerical degeneracy, formulation quality, or structure lost through user extensions before proposing a fix (p. 33).
Put ML inside a solver for one narrow interpretable decision (tree-size prediction for variable selection, cut-selection classifier) rather than end-to-end deep learning (p. 35).
coauthors: Report coordinated by C. Artigues, N. Brauner, P. Fouilhoux with 68 writers (p. 3); §B.2.2 written by 21 incl. Artigues, Prud'homme, Bonami, Berthold, Benoist, Perron, Besançon, Pacaud, Legat, Vanaret and Leyffer (p. 31).
